This version fixes some significant bugs <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/secr%204.1.0%20NEWS.txt> and extends the speed-up in 4.0 to include area searches (polygon detectors). It requires a recent version of R (>= 3.5.0), so you may need to update. messages.subject: null model error message
messages.body_plain:
Hi -

I am running into an error message that I haven't seen before. I have created my capthist file and everything checks out ok. I've looked at the summary information, plotted the mask, traps, tracks, etc. All looks good. However, when I run a null model:

m0 <- secr.fit(CHBM, model=list(D~1,g0~1,sigma~1), mask = maskBM, trace = FALSE)

I get the following warning message:
Warning message:
In dpois(data$nc, N * meanpdot, log = TRUE) : NaNs produced

When I look at the model output, the information is incorrect. The number of occasions is listed as 1 (there should be 140). Also, detector type is wrong - it is listed as "count" but should be "proximity."

Interestingly, when I add a covariate to either g0 or sigma (e.g. bk or T), things run correctly and there are no error messages. Also, in those cases the model output is correct (i.e. right number of occasions, correct detector type, etc.).

Any suggestions as to what might be going on with the null model?

Thanks
Andrea

messages.subject: Re: null model error message
messages.body_plain:
Firstly, these are not error messages. They are warnings.

I expect you are using secr 4.0.2 and should read about the changes between 3.2 and 4.0 <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-version4.pdf>. By default, compliant proximity data are compressed to a single count occasion before analysis with a binomial model. You can suppress the new behaviour by setting details = list(fastproximity = FALSE). I could have saved these headaches by making it default to the old behaviour, but I was dazzled by the speed of the new behaviour. Note also that bugs <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/secr%204.1.0%20NEWS.txt> in 4.0 have been fixed in 4.1 (on CRAN now but Windows binary lagging; find here <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_4.1.0.zip> if you're in a hurry).

The dpois warning is almost certainly innocuous - I expect it comes from a single likelihood evaluation early in maximization and has no effect on results.

Murray

messages.subject: Sampling design for a clustered population
messages.subject_clean: Sampling design for a clustered population
messages.body_plain:
We are studying an elk population that tends to be clustered around forest openings.  We are planning to use line transect sampling to collect and genotype elk scats for secr analysis.  Most of the elk fecal samples will be in these openings (fields) so we want to adequately sample those areas.  However, a random or systematic sampling design across elk range would result in us spending a lot of time in areas where there are few if any elk.  We have run some simulations with different sampling intensities in grid cells that we have designated as high density and low density, with greater sampling intensity in the high density cells.  The estimates seem okay with little bias.  However, my question is what if we are wrong in assigning the high density and low density cells?  For example, if high elk densities in reality extend further into the low density cells than we thought, will this present a bias?  So far, our simulations suggest no, but I was looking to see if there was a theoretical reason why this sampling approach might be flawed.

Alternatively, we were interested in estimating elk densities as a linear or quadratic function of the distance from fields.  I know that could be done, but would there be a bias if we adjusted our sampling effort the same way?  I know there are adaptive sampling approaches that might be used but I figured that since we have a pretty good idea that elk densities are going to be positively related to the fields, using that information to develop a sampling regime would be preferred.  Thanks!
Joe
